To enhance instruction accuracy in agent simulations, particularly when agents are being evaluated, it's important to clearly demonstrate the consequences of incorrect actions. We found that current environment designs fall short in this regard and presented an improved approach using external state modifications. This method effectively conveyed the effects of erroneous actions, as seen in a concrete example with an agent learning to navigate the Gridworld environment. We extended the original approach with a Markov Decision Process (MPC) to see if more intricate impacts could be effectively learned. Our experiments showed that this allowed for the successful incorporation of complex real-world scenarios, demonstrated through two case studies.

By matching numerical simulations of particle interactions to measured data, we have developed an exhaustive graphical representation of afterglows in varying environments. This representation, which is grounded in the underlying physics of the phenomenon, is particularly applicable to afterglows resulting from relativistic outflows that occur in a vacuum. By aligning the time of observation with a characteristic time frame, we can navigate this representation, which is divided into nine distinct regions. These regions are determined by the interaction of forward and radiative afterglows with various shock wave components. By comparing the representation to the temporal dynamics observed in the data, we found multiple correlations that are consistent with our initial hypotheses. Furthermore, we found that several temporal powers observed in the data are well-explained by the representation, which is particularly true for external radiation. However, we found that representation fails to explain the non-thermal distribution of temporal powers observed in the data. This initial representation of a complex phenomenon provides a foundation for understanding the underlying physics and for identifying areas of research that are likely to yield promising results.

It has been proven that for any graph G and integer k, we can efficiently find in a step-byropriate manner two subgraphs M and N belonging to G, such that M contains at most k query elements, N has a diameter of at least 2^p, and the combined size of M and N accounts for all of G's vertices.

This research investigates the potential of propulsion-assisted locomotion in bipedal creatures, examining how an external propulsor can enhance both efficiency and disaster resistance. A newly developed energy-optimal control method, tailored for a realistic robot with energy constraints and an indeterminate horizon, forms the basis of our analysis. Using an exhaustive search method, we examined how optimal travel distances and durations vary, finding that minimizing energy consumption results in an infinite travel duration at zero distance, with optimal durations and daily energy consumption rates determined in between. Furthermore, our study reveals how external disasters could cause optimal travel plans to fail, comparing this efficiency vulnerability to that of non-propulsive movements. To manage resilience, we propose that limited travel durations could be set, but this reduction would increase both actual energy consumption and daily energy consumption rates in minimal ways. A propulsion-assisted version of a well-known locomotion pattern is used to support our findings, demonstrating that optimal control durations are realistic and that resilience-limiting reduced durations may offer only a 5% increase in actual and daily consumption rates.

A respected valuation is assigned to a polynomial ring over a field, and the associated residue field is denoted as $\bar{k}$. For the polynomial ring, we identify the set of indices as $I$ associated with non-zero coefficients, and define the coefficient field's residue field $k$ as the product of these indices. The paper investigates the condition under which a complete residue map exists from the polynomial ring to the product of the associated indices. The existence of this map is characterized in the case where the respected valuation has a discrete value group. The condition is further explored when the valuation has an indefinite value group, and examples are provided to highlight the limitations and complexities of this scenario.

HyperDegrade is a new end-to-end rate throttling technique that aims to
rapidly recover from performance issues resulting in backlogged queues.
Existing throttle controllers focus solely on preventing queue build-up neglecting
the critical aspect of expeditiously recovering from such situations. In response,
HyperDegrage incorporates a novel two-phase approach that detects and responds to
network conditions with precision, utilizing an adaptive adjustable step-size
strategy to efficiently navigate through various scenarios. On top of this,
HyperDegrage significantly enhances performance by simultaneously adjusting multiple
system parameters to counter the side effects of reduced frequencies. Through
comprehensive simulations, HyperDegrage is shown to deliver remarkable
throughput, minimal queueing delays and frequency utilization in comparison to
existing methods.

This research investigates unknotting techniques for traditional and welded link types through the application of Conway polynomial properties. unconstrained movement of link crossings and endpoints is considered in our study to facilitate calculations. We demonstrate that the Conway polynomial coefficient patterns provide crucial information about traditional and welded link classifications and unknotting. While the first coefficient is consistently one, subsequent coefficients providing insights on the number of possible ways to decompose the link into simpler components, crossings that can be rearranged without altering the link's fundamental nature, and interactions between simpler unknotted components, respectively. Our analysis reveals that the presence of higher-order coefficients as fractions greater than one serves as an indicator of the link being classified as either traditional or welded, respectively, due to the ability to perform specific crossings or operations resulting in the formation of unknotted segments, thereby proving the uniqueness of these link types. Our research contributes to the understanding of how the Conway polynomial provides a profound means of detecting the nature of traditional and welded links and guiding strategies for their unknotting.

We demonstrate that the Fox-Hatcher loop constitutes a Vassiliev characteristic within the category of embedded circles in $\R^3$ for the third order, thereby resolving an open question originally posed by J. Przytycki and T. Traczyk in 1989. Furthermore, by drawing on insights from knot theory, we derive an explicitly formula for a certain singular function associated with the Vassiliev characteristic of order three, which helps resolve a challenge posed by V. Tognoli in 1969, showing that this function is not trivial.

In the Multi-Agent Delivery Competition, robotic teams navigate an intricate warehouse environment to collect and deliver food items while adhering to strict limitations on communication and computation. These agents operate within real-world constraints typical of unstructured logistics systems, presenting a study in multi-agent coordination. We analyzed the tactical collaboration potential of our successful multi-agent network, leveraging results from our competitive multi-agent reinforcement learning approach and tangible tactical cooperation strategies employed in the competition. Furthermore, we explored various tactical collaboration concepts, highlighting applicable and obstructive aspects for conventional multi-agent networks in structured settings.

This work examines the pragmatic privacy risks of three primary fluoride delivery methods used in vertical federated learning. It investigates how fluoride can be learned or inferred among participating servers through variable sample sizes. We provide fluoride reconstruction algorithms for scenarios where sample sizes are either known or uncertain. Our research reveals that this issue can be resolved by adjusting the process bars, but also highlights the fluoride's potential threat to data privacy in vertical federated education systems.

Traditional kernel methods struggle with high-dimensional data due to the computationally intensive nature of constructing kernel matrices. The creation of these matrices involves O(n^2) time and storing them consumes massive amounts of memory. To address this issue, we propose a novel kernel estimator called DPVR-F, which leverages pseudo-random Fourier attributes to reconstruct kernel values. The reconstruction accuracy of DPVR-F matches that of the original kernel while significantly reducing storage requirements and optimizing time complexity to O(n log n). Furthermore, the DPVR-based kernel method's memory consumption is substantially lower than the conventional method, consuming only a fraction of the memory. We validate the effectiveness of our proposal using real-world datasets and demonstrate its superior performance.

In recent years, interest in discrete group embeddings into product structures has surged. Notably, several group classes, including right-angled Artin groups, Sarvotam complexes, and Baumslag-Solitar groups, can be embedded into Garland products of type $\tilde{A}$. This paper's research builds upon the Cartesian Decomposition framework to achieve such embeddings. Initially, we generalise the stable letter displacement property, extending the result of W. Whitten, and subsequently, we apply the Cartesian Decomposition framework to achieve our primary finding, which is the ability to embed right-angled Artin groups into product structures using disjunctive operations.
We prove a novel result regarding compact hypersurfaces within spherical space if their conformal class exhibits non-positive M\"obius curvature.

In a new type of wireless system that uses simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT), there's a conflict between supplying energy and transmitting data because power beams from the base station (BS) to the device are not the same. This document explores SWIPT in an OFDMA system using a model where part of the signal is dedicated to providing energy and the remaining section is for data transmission. This approach is limited by how much energy can be harvested and how much data rate can be achieved. Based on these constraints, various SWIPT resource distribution methods are investigated to determine the data rate that can be successfully transmitted. It is also investigated how changing the fraction of energy harvested affects this data rate. Furthermore, an example is presented where the SWIPT system is success-orientated instead of rate-orientated in order to transmit a certain packet successfully. Ultimately, notable implications of these findings for novel applications of SWIPT technology are discussed.

A. F. Kemper discovered an intriguing pattern in prime factorizations of Cayley graph numbers, suggesting that the natural logarithms of individual factors form a declining sequence resembling an exponential distribution when analyzed in a two-dimensional space. To understand this phenomenon, we created a probabilistic model using randomly selected generators and found it accurately replicates the logarithmic spacing of the factors in our model as well. However, when we modified the model to match the often seen complex graph structures with multiple cycles, our simulation results deviated from our initial probabilistic prediction.

The detection sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors is influenced by several factors, including their ability to respond to rapid phenomena. The detector LIGO is anticipated to experience a significant event, following which the mirror attached to an isolated mass responds sluggishly due to its existing design, potentially interfering with the detector's data during critical periods. The proposed innovation, known as the 'sloshing Sagnac' configuration, is predicted to enhance the high-frequency response of these detectors by decoupling the detector's response time from the response of the isolated mass. The current design of the interferometer leads to a discrepancy in frequency response between the two arms, which constrines its overall response, but the proposed 'sloshing' Sagnac design resolves this issue by employing an additional beam splitter and isolated masses arrangement. Analytical, numerical, and experimental methods all confirm the proposed design's effectiveness in responding to gravitational phenomena by facilitating the rapid response of both interferometer arms through different isolated mass responses.

This research focuses on an new aspect of space foraging in extreme large MIMO (Massive) systems, examining a scenario where signal-based intersection detection misleads devices about their proximity to access points in an unstructured access protocol. We find that in many cases, two spatially separated devices can occupy the same free bandwidth without conflicting with each other, thus allowing for a safe simultaneous data transmission. A quantitative analysis was conducted to estimate the probability of such non-intersecting visibility areas (NIVAs), and a method was proposed to exploit this phenomenon to increase the total network throughput. Our proposed algorithm, Exploiting Non-Intersected Visibility Areas (E-NIVA), utilizes the unique capabilities of extreme large MIMO systems to optimize network data transmission, and simulation results show a notable improvement in overall network throughput when E-NIVA is applied.

Recent submillimeter observations at high resolution have revealed that a significant number of galaxy disks appear to be fragmented into short-scale structures. While some of these features could be attributed to spiral arm patterns caused by gravitational interactions or internal instabilities, understanding their true nature is complicated, particularly since a novel instability, vertical shear instability (VSI), was recently discovered to potentially contribute to heating and structure formation in galaxy disks with short lifespans. To assess the likelihood of VSI playing a pivotal role in shaping these galaxies, a computational study combining two-dimensional hydrodynamical modeling and radiative transfer modeling has been undertaken. Our model incorporates two primary sources of structure formation instability: VSI and gravitational instability. We specifically focused on radii where life-sustaining planets are most likely to be found in gas giant systems and predicted that regions exhibiting intense submillimeter emissions with at least three standard deviations above the average are more likely to be located outside of the habitable zone. Conversely, we anticipate that regions within one radius outside of the mid-zone are more likely to exhibit emissions indicators corresponding to a local intensity of at least one standard deviation above the average. Conversely, regions that are compact, likely confined to less than one radius, are more likely to exhibit very weak or suppressed submillimeter structures. Such distinctive emission patterns may serve as reliable markers of regions with high gas temperatures in galaxy disks, thus assisting in the assessment of the potential prevalence of life-sustaining planets in various exoplanetary systems.

A novel axial vector diquark interaction has been incorporated into the Relativistic Quark Model to enhance its descriptive capabilities for a wide range of hadronic matter states. By utilizing this enhanced model, researchers calculated the mass spectra for both mesons and baryons in a variety of astronomical objects, from the earliest universe to neutron stars. Notably, the model accurately predicted the critical baryon density where matter transitions from quark-gluon plasma to quark matter in the early universe. Also, the model's results aligned perfectly with experimental data obtained from particle accelerators regarding the relationship between pressure and energy density of quark matter. The results further indicated that quark matter could form stable astronomical objects in the early universe and within neutron stars, as well as predicting the existence of quark stars and hybrid stars. Moreover, the model's calculations revealed that the most compact type of matter within neutron stars is dense mesons rather than bare quarks, and it even allowed for the estimation of the maximum size of a big apple.

This research focuses on implementing robust Molmer-Sorensen gates for a variety of isotopic ions using a coherent electromagnetic field to link their atomic connections and magnetic field gradients to decouple their spins. By selecting optimal gauge settings and input signal parameters, we demonstrate the possibility of achieving highly reliable quantum logic gates, resistant to temperature fluctuations and gauge imperfections, with an infidelity as low as $10^{-4}$. Furthermore, these gates can be executed efficiently on a collection of more than a dozen consecutive ions within a time frame of 100 microseconds to 200 microseconds at a low cost of at least 99.6% fidelity, even on a set of 20 or more ions across two distinct trapped molecular ions systems. By streamlining the necessary equipment, this approach could significantly reduce the cost of building a quantum computer based on trapped ion technology.

Using a non-trivial magnetoelectric response in spin-orbit coupled insulators with missing layers, we theoretically describe a (d+1)-dimensional Dirac metal that exhibits exceptionally high conductivity. In a two examples, known as the Hofstadter multilayer and the hexagonal multilayer, perpendicular electric fields induce exceptional Hall conductivity and giant circular Hall effect. This results in extremely high DC Hall conductivity in both DC and AC regimes. Our findings highlight the potential for highly efficient Hall devices in these multilayer structures.

We have computed the anticipated NA62 experiment results for a potential new neutral lepton type, which could minimally arise in certain theoretical frameworks. In this calculation, we took into consideration both the measured $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay rate along with constraints from $CP$ asymmetry in $B^0 \to \phi K^*^0$ decay, while also considering recent findings from CHARM II and NA49 experiments. Our calculation can directly compare with current NA62 data, potentially revealing signs of a new neutral lepton type.

Our hypothesis that neurons in modern large-scale neural language models (NLLMs) function similarly to traditional $n$-gram models, yet distribute their outputs across different dimensions, has led us to develop a novel neural language technique. We found that by training the networks to replicate human language without an reference to written text, they effectively capture the underlying structural knowledge of our linguistic system. We demonstrate this approach, which we call the Residual $n$-gram Model (RnG), achieves state-of-the-results on a range of standard neural language generation tasks, surpassing current leading techniques, particularly as the size of the dataset grows. We believe our study offers both a defensible moral alternative to using neural networks for generating text and valuable insights into the technical effectiveness of them for the same purpose. We also present visual evidence from visual analyses that supports our fundamental theoretical concept that underlies our technique.

This research paper presents a novel approach to robust face reconstruction in three-dimensional space, addressing the challenges posed by the sensitivity of current methods to facial feature detection failures on highly irregular faces. Our key innovation, Self-Aligned Dual Networks (SADR), comprises two tightly coupled face detection and reconstruction models that refine each other's predictions iteratively, mitigating detection errors through localized coordinate transformations. Our iterative refinement process involves: (1) aligning undetected regions of the current framework, and (2) updating undetected areas of the current model. Our method, SADR, has been experimentally evaluated under challenging conditions and demonstrates notable improvements over current state-of-the-art techniques, accurately localizing and reconstructing previously problematic, loosely constrained faces. Our dataset, comprising over 10,000 manually marked and unrestrained face images, is also made available to the research community.

In our study, we investigate the fluctuations generated during $\alpha$-attractor inflation, focusing on a specific model with $N_F$ fields and an $R^2$ term, and determine the conditions required for the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). We find that in the standard scenario where the fields interact with an Einstein-term, PBHs can only form during the early universe's radiation-dominated period. Conversely, in models with an $R^2$ term, PBHs can also form in the early universe's matter-dominated period. We conclude that the rare decay of a large PBH into $N_F$ particles could provide an effective mechanism for matter to radiation energy transfer in the early universe.

For the labeled ordered trees with n+1 nodes numbered 1 through n+1, we identify the latest node added to form the tree and denote it as the deepest node, with its position marked as the deepest index. Our analysis of these trees reveals that the count of nodes up to and including the deepest index, let's call it D, conforms to a specific distribution. Interestingly, this distribution matches the well-known Catalan structure. Moreover, we establish additional characteristics of the deepest index, index, and find that the probability of the deepest index being at position k aligns with a particular formula, again reminiscent of the Catalan numbers. Furthermore, we extend our study to incorporate a more intricate tree formation process, known as the Piterbarg construction, and determine analogous properties for the deepest index in this context. Additionally, our ordered labeled trees can be mapped to sorted 231-avoiding permutations, and the properties of the deepest index and index apply to these permutations as well.

This investigation utilizes actual data from an election results processing system, 
which automatically processes images of machine-scanned voter records. To enhance 
the current performance of these systems, we propose a performance improvement 
strategy for algorithms that interpret these scans. We evaluate this approach 
empirically using real-world data from the 2019 French elections and discover that 
a simple implementation of our method significantly outperforms the current Hamming 
distance algorithm, which is widely used in these systems. Furthermore, our results 
indicate that these systems have sufficient performance margins to safely apply this 
informed algorithm.

In time series analysis, a scenario known as the "benign misfitting" phenomenon occurs when an under-specifying model produces parameter estimates that converge to zero despite the true data-generating process being linear and well-specified. This paper, which examines an highly over-parameterized least squares method for linear regression on stationary time series, finds that such a bizarre outcome does in fact happen under certain conditions where variables are pre-processed using sample means and residuals. Our study establishes theoretical bounds for regression performance and provides numerical demonstrations of the proposed method's performance.

This research explores storage operation strategies in a multi-market environment from the perspective of risk aversion. Using Markov decision theory, we establish a risk-sensitive mathematical model to establish an optimal storage operation strategy. Through a statistical linearization method, we analytically approximate a risk-sensitive mathematical model. Furthermore, we compare our theoretical findings with simulated results, validate our approach through Monte Carlo simulations, and examine storage operation policies across different market scenarios and risk levels in a casual discussion.

A simplified radiative equilibrium model of planetary atmospheres features a range of circulation patterns that depend on scale. These patterns can be understood by considering three primary forces: the Coriolis effect, the cyclostrophic force, and turbulence, which become relevant in different regions of radius. As a result, the prevailing balance of forces that shapes the atmospheric circulation varies across different types of planets within the same orbital distance range. Furthermore, a particular range of temperatures and radii is found where the atmospheric circulation exhibits particularly complex and unpredictable behavior. This range shifts to higher temperatures as temperatures required for the emergence of life increase, indicating a potential barrier to life's development due to complex atmospheric dynamics rather than the habitable zone concept based on temperature. Our analysis of this model reveals intricate relationships between atmospheric dynamics and the probability of life's development, providing a more nuanced understanding of where life may or may not arise.

Deep neural networks are often trained on fixed machine learning datasets to foster network performance. Our group's research explores a more adaptive approach where a neural network actively decides which samples to learn from in order to maximize performance. Most prior dynamic learning studies involve networks that choose samples from static datasets. We examine a fully dynamic learning setting where the neural network not only selects samples but also must instruct a human annotator to generate new labels for newly created class labels, in real-time. Consequences of this constant label space growth must be managed in terms of both performance and computational efficiency. We propose a novel model to handle this challenge called a Dynamic Neural Learner that sets new sample selection and retention strategies, and employs an optimized projection method for efficient inference. Our model's performance is assessed via simulated experiments based on a realistic setting with high-scale data akin to ImageNet, showing that it outperforms current methods in this domain.

Researchers have utilized a precise theoretical approach called multi-valley effective weight theory to thoroughly examine the quantum states of specific configurations of silicon-based spin qubits. These specific configurations include an interstitial donor ($In$) and an electron ($e$)$, as well as another electron donor pair consisting of two electrons located at a donor site ($P$). Through these simulations, they exchanged interactions within these systems were examined in detail across various possible arrangements of the electrons at the $Ine$ and $PP$ donor locations. To accurately represent the exchange interactions in the $PP$ configuration, the theory incorporated multiple multi-valley components, revealing previously unobserved phenomena such as the coexistence of split-valley and localized multi-valley states, which can influence the behavior of quantum computers built using silicon-based technology.

Our theoretical investigation examines the transport properties of a specific type of two-dimensional particle transport known as Dirac particles, which occur in HgTe quantum trenches where the thickness is less than 5.8 nm. Based on experimental data from closed quantum trenches of this type, our study resolves the mystery of the conductance observed near the charge neutrality point by demonstrating that it is caused by the scattering of electrons and holes at impurities, resulting in weak localization effects. Furthermore, we provide a method for determining the size of these impurities and determining the orientation of their atomic dipoles. Notably, we discover that when an external magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the material, the effects of weak localization give way to quantum anomalous Hall states with opposite directions for electrons and holes, and these states disappear when the magnetic field is removed. Furthermore, we find that these electron and hole states exhibit enhanced sensitivity to in-plane magnetic fields compared to graphene, and this phenomenon vanishes when the magnetic field is removed. All of these findings are supported by first-principles calculations and can be directly observed in weak localization effects.

In this study, a novel Machine Learning-based Model Allocation Algorithm for Uplink and Downlink frequency segments in Dynamic TDD networks is presented, addressing the rapid growth of mobile data usage. By allowing flexible uplink and downlink assignments, 5G networks can better serve varying traffic patterns but also face synchronization challenges across base stations. To address this, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning approach is proposed, enabling an efficient and coordinated allocation of uplink and downlink models, and and mathematical proof of convergence is provided. Simulations demonstrate that this algorithm outperforms existing ML-based methods and ensures synchronized operation of Base Stations, a critical requirement for Dynamic TDD operation.

In this work, we introduce a novel architecture for Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) that recovers gradients of state variables through a theoretically proven method, eliminating the need for labeled trajectory data. Our method applies to universal approximators of sine and cosine functions, and we demonstrate its success with a specific set of Bessel functions of the first kind. HNNs are valuable tools for training neural ODE solvers in various applications, particularly when state variables cannot be directly measured. To validate our approach, we conducted numerical experiments comparing our model to existing HNN structures in scenarios where the training data lacks velocity information.

A proposed approach integrates a set of data labels provided by a human for each feature within an dataset, along with a set of features that can be inputted directly, before a machine learning algorithm starts training. This human element continuously supplies feedback on the reliability of the predicted output of the model, utilizing a interface that facilitates real-time interactions with a set of other agents representing different users. Based on this interface, humans can interface with the system to assess the reliability of predicted outputs, with a five-star rating scale similar to that used for service reviews. We believe this method yields a high-quality set of data labels and allows for target enrichment, which can be utilized to train a classification algorithm that predicts reliability scores for new instances, which in turn can be interfaces with the system before the model produces a final prediction. This human-element is crucial for enhancing the robustness and generalization capabilities of the system, with studies conducted across different scenarios highlighting the benefits of this approach, including a case study involving real-world data from insurance agents in a data brokerage firm.

We modify the quantum invariant of 2-chains within the cylinder $T^2 \times I$, developed by Kassel and Tognoli, to produce quantities that mirror the second moment of a normal distribution, under specific conditions. Our construction relies on redefining the evaluation of a particular 2-chain, representing a torus with a colored knot hole, the value of which increases in direct proportion to the resistance encountered in an electrical circuit with capacitors and resistors configured in a star-delta transformation.

This paper delves into the challenge of resolving the ambiguity of word meanings in both literal and neural semantic disambiguation contexts, focusing on the availability of contextual information in these scenarios. We divide the context available to a semantic disambiguation model into three sub-contexts: document, paragraph, and sentence, and investigate the significance of each context type. Our research highlights the substantial influence of sentence-level information and facilitates the optimization of semantic disambiguation models by emphasizing the incorporation of textual embeddings. Furthermore, we develop a novel context-gloss enhancement framework consisting of three main components: data annotation, labeling, and fusion, and conduct extensive experiments using diverse datasets and pre-trained models. The results indicate the effectiveness of our approach when compared to existing methods. Additionally, we find interesting results that reveal the varying significance of different context levels across different sentences and senses.

This study explores a reciprocal Gamma function, denoted as $1/\Gamma(z)$, and establishes several integral representations, including a two-dimensional and a one-dimensional form. It is demonstrated that $1/\Gamma(z)$ can be expressed as an integral over the real line in the shape $\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(w) e^{zw} \, d_w$, where $f$ belongs to specific function spaces. Furthermore, it is proven that the reciprocal Gamma function is uniquely determined by this condition.

Our topQuench model successfully predicts the production of single top quarks in proton-nucleus interactions, particularly in large nuclei like lead. Our calculations closely match experimental data from the CMS at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=8$ TeV for single top quark transverse momentum distributions in $pp$ and $p{\rm Pb}$ collisions. We also found that the average transverse momentum of top quarks is higher in $p{\rm Pb}$ collisions compared to $pp$ collisions, with a 10-20% greater difference than for associated Higgs boson production. Our topQuench approach provides a viable explanation for the transverse momentum difference observed by the CMS collaboration.

Integrating database queries across domains with different structures is essential for creating unified data presentations and decision-support systems. While current solutions combine individual queries manually or automatically, they focus primarily on schema compatibility, neglecting the parsing difficulty that varies between domains. This challenge is compounded when dealing with a target domain that lacks sufficient data for effective model training. In response, we introduce a novel support-assisted cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing framework, addressing both domain differences and low-resource scenarios. Our framework uses a support-assisted setup with two key assumptions: the target and source domains differ only in table names, and a shared underlying question is expressed similarly across domains. Building on these assumptions, we develop a four-stage framework consisting of a pre-parser, support encoder, matcher, and parser. Experimentation on the Spider benchmark demonstrates the effectiveness of our framework, achieving a 0.85 match set F1 score in both cross-domain and single-domain settings, outperforming baselines significantly. Our results also highlight the potential of cross-domain learning and emphasize the importance of difficulty generalization in text-to-SQL parsers. To support further research, we will openly share the training and validation datasets for both single-domain and cross-domain settings.

This discussion delves into the complexities of preserving privacy in social network analysis. Social networks are represented as graphs in this context, and we examine various confidential computing techniques meant to protect sensitive data within these networks. We focus particularly on common graph structures such as adjacency matrices, triangle lists, and the Column-Simplified Diagonal Triangular list (CSDTL). Our study explores several transformation processes including sampling, truncation, one-time encryption, reordering, shifting, and truncation with reordering. Our analysis reveals that none of these processes meet the strictest privacy standards of differential confidentiality (DC). To address this issue, we propose new graph processes designed to maintain data privacy while facilitating social network analysis. Our proposed solutions are applicable to a wide range of social network operations including anonymous messaging platforms like Snapchat and Twitter, and facilitates analysis of relationships among people, including those used by dating services and law enforcement investigations.

A new stochastic approach has been developed to derive the quantum hydrodynamics equations, extending space-based random phase theory to incorporate interparticle interactions within a Bose fluid. In this method, the fluid's macroscopic variables are treated as deterministic variables within a phase-space framework, while super-phase space variables represent space-based random phase variables. Building on Landau and Lifshitz space-based random phase theory, this approach uses variable transformation to linearize the non-linear hydrodynamics equations. By applying the requirement that super-average field variables must remain linear deterministic variables, the quantum hydrodynamics equations are obtained. This approach is shown to be equivalent to the Madelain transformation when applied to a non-interacting case. Furthermore, it provides the quantum hydrodynamics equations, specifically the GPE, in terms of coarse-grained super-phase space variables. This approach provides a more robust basis for developing semi-classical numerical methods.

We develop extensive deviation principles for the asymptotic behavior of a letter in a word $w$, a letter in a k-letter word $w \in A_k^n$, and a specific k-tuple in a letter sequence $X^n$. These concepts explore the frequency of particular letters or combinations within the given sequences. Traditional results, primarily established by Chou, Levinson, and Szabo, are founded on the notion of a random word or sequence, yet we extend our analysis to apply to deterministic letter sequences, providing a more comprehensive understanding of their asymptotic properties.

Let $M$ be an arbitrary Riemannian manifold and $h$ be a given homotopy type on $M$. We define a metric, denoted as $\mathcal{D}_h$, on the set of all homotopy types defined on $M$. This paper explores the concept of a subspace $\Gamma_h \subset \mathcal{A}_+^1(M)$ that consists of all 1-boundary-free functions on $M$ and minimizes the metric $\mathcal{D}_h$ within this space. We investigate the properties of a function $F_h \subset \mathcal{A}_+^1(M)$ that consists of all functions that minimize the metric $\mathcal{D}_h$ for some element in $\Gamma_h$. For a specific class of metrics, it is proven that the set of all minimizing functions is non-empty and compact. This result is analogous to a recent discovery by Casselman and Simon (2022) for the space of all Riemannian currents in metric spaces that minimize the distance to a given homotopy type in a metric space.

This paper introduces the J-K fold cross-validation technique, an innovative variation of conventional cross-validation, and demonstrates its effectiveness in refining neural network models for various N sub-tasks. traditional cross-validation utilizes the entire training data for both model adjustment and parameter validation, which can increase the risk of overfitting and variance. In contrast, our method ensures that the model and validation sets are independent by employing different instances, thereby reducing variance and improving model performance. Furthermore, we discuss the limitations of the J-K fold technique and present potential solutions.

Recently, human-involvement knowledge acquisition strategies have seen significant success, as they are suitable for embedding generalistic knowledge bases and addressing complex situations. Human-prioritization knowledge acquisition frameworks have emerged as a subdivision of these strategies, as they capitalize on the strengths of generative models while leveraging the capabilities of humans to rectify and fine-tune predictions. This paper discusses various knowledge acquisition processes that center around humans, including supervised settings, semi-supervised approaches, active learning, and game theoret models. A novel classification process is introduced, categorizing these strategies into three main processes: initial generation, human correction, and mutual improvement. A distinct inquiry into several knowledge-constructs that can be established between humans and generative models is examined in this framework, leading to a comprehensive assessment of current knowledge-constructs and highlighting opportunities for future research. A instructor-pupil framework is proposed as a research direction, highlighting the potential for mutual-improvement knowledge-constructs to be realized through these frameworks.

We present a fundamental approach to computing the most probable explanation in a Markov random field through graphical models, using the standard sum-product algorithm. We demonstrate that the same computational framework employed for marginal inference in a model can also be utilized to determine the most probable explanation in that model. We establish the relationship between the most probable explanation and the sum-product algorithm, showing that the standard approach involving instance scores and message aggregation in each factor and variable node, respectively, generates sufficient information to calculate the most probable explanation in an identical graphical structure with the same operations. We further extend our method to directed acyclic graphs by utilizing the same sum-product algorithm to compute the most probable explanation in such models.

To confirm that photon recoil results in a measurable frequency shift of 385 Hz, we observed the absorption features of counter-propagating beams traveling in opposite directions. Our observations of the Doppler widths and shapes of the absorption spectra provided us with the necessary data to quantify the impact of photon recoil, although we found the detected Doppler widths to be significantly broader than theoretical predictions of 1.85 cm$^{-1}$. To better understand the root cause of this discrepancy, we attempted to measure the velocity distribution of the vapor using an ultracentrifuge and found the resulting Doppler widths to be very similar to those measured via absorption spectroscopy. When a shear-aligned polymer melt reaches a critical point, it transforms from an elliptical to a circular cross-section under the influence of increasing shear flow. To investigate the phenomena occurring during this transition, researchers employed both theoretical analysis and numerical studies using the Knudsen number as a key parameter. Initially studied for pressure-driven flows in rectangular channels, this number has now been utilized for shear flow between parallel plates. Although the scaling relations observed for this transition appear similar to those for the alignment threshold, further investigation is necessary to fully understand the similarities and differences between the two processes, as well as the underlying mechanisms at play.

These algebras, which have inherent properties of Clifford and Heisenberg-Weyl algebras, provide a foundational framework for a novel quantization technique of combinatorial models. Google's Web search personalization is likely influencing its users' knowledge. This study aims to explicitly demonstrate how personalization distacts the amount of relevant information that can be perceived. It utilizes innovative equipment to instantly gather web search history, allowing for direct correlations between past, present, and future search histories. To achieve this, 183 U.S. volunteers used Google's Web search both before and after being exposed to neutral and positively charged content, with their worldviews tested using the Worldview Scale. Findings indicate that past and future search histories are highly correlated, especially for individuals with open worldviews. Furthermore, their worldviews affect their susceptibility to in-formations' perceived importance. This implies that Google's Web search personalization leads to missing out on important information. Its implications are far-reaching, particularly in regards to possible gender differences in this effect's magnitude.

A new type of particle accelerator, featuring a 1 TeV muon beam and colliding it with 25 TeV proton beams from the Future Circular Collider (FCC), has been found to provide significant advantages in certain physics research areas. These include studying the Higgs boson and exotic particles with high precision, as well as exploring quantum chromodynamics at the forefront, particularly in multi-jet and top quark production. Calculations and simulations have shown that this muon-ion accelerator can offer unprecedented data for various processes and has been found to be particularly effective in certain research domains. Furthermore, the feasible production of such a high-energy muon beam has been demonstrated using an existing design for a proton beam line, highlighting the potential for a practical 1 TeV muon-ion accelerator.

We present a novel approach, a motion-adjusted reconstruction method based on an enhanced model of the signal generation process in MRI, to address the issues of breathing-related artifacts in 4D (specifically 3D MRI plus respiratory effects) T2-weighted sequences. This method is applicable to a wide range of applications, including endorectal and pelvic MRI. In our research, we acquired two sets of data via MRI: a free-breathing T2-weighted sequence and a respiratory-triggered T2-weighted sequence on the same individuals. We then used a spiral-encoding technique to obtain undistorted images and applied a sophisticated algorithm to realign Free-breathing images across different slices of an echo train, based on the characteristics of the signal generation in MRI. This allowed us to create high-quality, high-resolution Free-breathing images free from breathing-related distortions. To evaluate the effectiveness of this method, we compared the motion-adjusted free-breathing images with the respiratory-triggered images on nine subjects' data. The results showed that the motion-adjusted images provided accurate and detailed image quality and better image registration with the respiratory-triggered images. Automatic text assessment methods rely on structured metrics computed from semantic representations. These metrics exhibit strong correlations with human judgments ondecomposed components such as similarity and intelligibility. To examine how metrics like similarity and intelligibility contribute to the overall performance, a paired-permutation testing framework was developed. This framework enables the precise evaluation of structure metric components' influence on overall metric performance. According to our findings, similarities between decoded representations significantly influence commonly used structured metrics like similarity and sum of absolute differences, and this influence varies depending on the specific metric employed.

This research provides comprehensive statistics on cargo shipping costs, supply, and capital appreciation within the bulk cargo shipping industry spanning 30 years (1966-1995) on a global scale, filling a data gap identified in previous studies which only had limited annual data from 1973-1975 and 1980, with 5-year interval data otherwise. Such contiguous yearly data is crucial for econometric analysis of the bulk cargo shipping sector. Our findings reveal that shipping prices were generally negotiable, with published rates serving as rate ceilings, largely influenced by individual shipping agreements and market conditions. A Bayesian average equation was developed using disparate data sets to determine prices, supply, and the supply's price elasticity in the new bulk cargo shipping ship market. Our results suggest that the stock of new ships was primarily driven by installed capacity with a 0.075 estimated price elasticity, whereas the scrap supply was found to be perfectly elastic at zero. Additionally, we identified and compared international bulk cargo shipping sector patterns across different data sources and simulated impacts of missing data intervals.

Gehring and Lehto introduced the concept of fabric spaces in the late 1960s, which were redefined by Osherman using convex hulls in 2002. This paper extends Lehto's initial ideas, presenting diverging triangulations to give a new example of fabric spaces. We prove that the tip set of a diverging triangulation maintains its shape under the Stern-Rockin operation, providing an invariant under this operation. Additionally, this concept can be applied to understand the geometric properties of hyperbolic and Euclidean operators within the monoid of all natural number operators.

We explore how to predict the future of company success, leveraging large
data sets and individual news articles from press releases to reputable
sources like Bloomberg. Using BERT models and a stock price dataset spanning
ten years for ten well-known companies, we employ various techniques to
refine the BERT model for ranking and predicting the implicit value of
organizations. We enhance the ranking BERT model's performance through
strategically selected loss functions and leveraged class frequencies, addressing
common issues in handling class-imbalance problems. We also integrate the
TSM-BiLSTM-GAN model to counter data lack and volatility, facilitating more
accurate implicit value ranking and forecasting. Computational results
demonstrate that this approach yields superior outcomes compared to existing
methods in terms of implicit value ranking and performance forecasting.

To assess the sensitivity with which Next Generation $e^+e^-$ colliders can probe Higgs effective field theory, we calculate double Higgs production processes, utilizing two models of non-standard Higgs physics: the dimension-7 Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) and the scalar effective field theory (SEFT). We determine the dimensions at which new physics could become observable in experiments at CLIC and FCC-ee, focusing on a specific SEFT parameter and the dimension-7 SMEFT parameter. We find that CLIC can detect SEFT effects beginning at the 10 TeV**2** scale and SMEFT effects at the 30 TeV**2** scale if they result in visible cross-section deviations from the Standard Model (SM). For particular SM+SEFT and SM+SMEFT parameter configurations, we determine that the FCC-ee can identify effects at 5 TeV**2} and 15 TeV**2}, respectively, whereas CLIC can do so at 30 TeV**2} and beyond, reflecting their differing luminosities at their high-intensity channels.

We begin by examining the fundamental stresses associated with a classical gravitational field, leading to the formulation of suitable Lagrangians. As gravity is inherently tensorial and non-dispersive, appropriate model Lagrangians demand the inclusion of second-order derivatives within the metric within a non-dispersive framework. After presenting several examples of suitable Lagrangians for a classical gravitational field, we then derive the corresponding equations of motion for matter fields in this context.

This study investigates the forward and backward drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a fluid-filled granular bed both with and without fluid flow. Observations indicate that backward drag exceeds forward drag for the cylinder as flow velocity, cylinder length relative to bed depth, and cylinder surface roughness increase. Notable asymmetypes in drag were observed in a fluid-filled bed without flow but not in a dry bed. High-speed video analysis reveals that forward and backward drag results from the interaction of cylinder-induced flow with the bed surface waves created by cylinder movement. Backward drag is influenced by the depth of fluid, the depth of the bed, and the roughness of the cylinder's surface. This research has implications for biologists studying organisms that live on sediments and for engineers designing sediment transport models.

Our research utilizes an event generator based on the multiphase transport model to analyze initial anisotropic fluctuations and their impact on higher-order anisotropic flow, specifically $v_n$, in heavy-ion collisions. By comparing simulations of 20 GeV Au+Au collisions at RHIC, we found a strong correlation between second anisotropic flow ($v_2$) and nucleon position fluctuations along the collision axis, which led to a significant connection between elliptical flow and triangular flow (between $v_2$ and $v_3$). Conversely, with increased transverse momentum, this relationship weakened due to radial momentum anisotropy ($v_2(p_T)$) playing a more pronounced role. Additionally, our study found that collisions with lower centrality or $p_T$ exhibited a higher $v_2$-$\langle v_3\rangle / v_2$ correlation, whereas collisions with higher centrality or $p_3$ had lower values of this ratio due to initial geometric fluctuations diminishing as the system approached its thermodynamic limit. Furthermore, our model accurately captured experimental observations of a lower $v_2$-$\langle v_3\rangle / v_2$ ratio in more central Cu+Cu collisions compared to more peripheral Cu+Cu collisions, in the same collision energy.

The ATLAS collider experiment has sought signs of uncommon decay processes and potential indications of new physics beyond the Standard Model in beauty mesons, addressing areas previously unexplored in hadronic decay domains. This report consolidates recent findings from ATLAS in two areas of research: measurements of neutral $B$-meson decay rates into two photons and an attempt to capture any source of physics-induced symmetry violation, known as CP, in $B^0$ decays into two photons.

We investigate the effectiveness of preconditioned Krylov subspace solvers for the numerical solution of first-order hyperbolic conservation laws using the WHAM discontinuous Galerkin method on unstructured meshes. Initially, this paper builds upon the WHAM code, a high-resolution, cell-centred DG solver designed for both linear and non-linear hyperbolic conservation laws on unstructured meshes, by integrating a DG formulation that mirrors the WHAM algorithm. Subsequently, this DG variant is reformulated to utilize an upper triangular matrix structure, facilitating efficient application within unstructured mesh environments. Numerical experiments are presented to assess the suitability of various preconditioners for DG solvers and demonstrate the DG-WHAM hybrid approach for solving complex 2D and 3D mesh problems with extended time steps.

Radiation therapy treatment verification poses significant challenges due to tumor and normal tissue invisible effects, which may indicate a non-rigid deformation posing a risk of tumor shift or expansion into healthy areas. For accurate target realignment, it's crucial to understand and model these deformations, particularly in complex anatomical regions like the head and neck. In this context, we introduce a novel non-rigid registration method based on a patient-specific finite element model of anatomy, which incorporates individualized biomechanical properties and boundary conditions to efficiently match a pre-treatment anatomical model with real-time imaging. This approach allows for the identification of non-rigid deformations and their relationship to anatomical features, thus facilitating target realignment for subsequent treatment. Our results demonstrate the method's capability to accurately recreate MRI images from an FE model, providing reliable information on internal anatomy for further therapeutic procedures.

LiDAR-based autonomous vehicles need accurate scene flow estimation to effectively detect and predict the movement of moving objects. Recent advancements in this field have primarily been driven by data annotation, but this approach is limited by the difficulty of labeling point cloud sequences accurately. A more practical alternative is self-supervised flow annotation, which has developed various intermediate annotation methods to bridge the gap between simple annotations and precise flow annotations. This category of annotations includes neighbor flow labels, but research reveals their reliability to be compromised by inaccuracy and introduces complex errors that hinder the performance of subsequent models. Although numerous studies attempt to address this issue, their success heavily depends on dense LiDAR data, which poses challenges for real-world applications. In a novel approach, our team presents a novel metric learning framework called NAST, which estimates inter-point flow distances based on their semantic relationships and temporal correlations. Experimental results show that the proposed method significantly surpasses recent comparative methods in a wide range of real-world scenarios.

This paper investigates the potential of Analog Spiking Neural Network (SNN) for efficient image classification, specifically with a focus on using Random Neural Network (RNN) for energy conservation and speed. Although previous studies have highlighted the advantages of using analog RNN in classification tasks, there are concerns regarding noise interference and the potential decrease in performance over time due to the inherently stochastic nature of the algorithm. To tackle these challenges, we propose an innovative hybrid architecture that combines digital and analog components, allowing for initial feature extraction with an energy-intensive camera, followed by feature reduction and classification using the low-power RNN algorithm on the sensor. Our results, obtained through various applications, showcase the efficiency of this approach, specifically with the use of a MobileEye sensor and an RGB-D camera on the rKIT dataset, showing up to an 80% reduction in energy consumption and 5 times faster inference speed compared to the conventional fully connected neural network algorithm. Our findings also highlight the suitability of Random Neural Network for real-time object recognition tasks, showcasing its potential for sustainable and high-performance applications.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of a spin-aligned strange quark star in the presence of a strong magnetic field at high temperatures. A novel model has been developed to describe the equation of state for these stars, combining the Maxwell's formalism to handle the transition between hadronic and quark phases within a strong magnetic field. The effects of temperature, quark mass, and the magnetic field on the structure of these stars have been analyzed by solving the modified Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations. According to our findings, an increase in temperature can lead to a transformation from a hadronic star to a strange quark star, and then back to a hadronic star at extremely high temperatures; an increase in the magnetic field strength results in a compression of the stellar structure; and in the presence of a strong magnetic field, axial chemical potential stars exhibit unlike behavior compared to their aligned counterparts.

This research builds upon the concept of pairings in graph theory, focusing on a specific type of graph where every vertex connects to exactly three others with different colored links. We define an ideal pairing within these graphs, demonstrating that they are highly specific and rigid structures. Furthermore, each such graph containing these ideal pairings can form an unbroken Hamiltonian circuit. When we remove one colored link from these graphs, they are able to recover their original structure. In contrast, when we attempt to add a colored link to any well-connected graph with exactly three links per vertex, they are also capable of maintaining this property. These findings are illustrated using examples.

The burgeoning popularity of containerized microservices is driving significant interest, yet the scale of this growth poses safety concerns and challenges in ensuring the reliability of these systems. To address this issue, we aim to automate the creation of system call rules for containerized microservices. To achieve this, we have developed a novel framework called Timeloops, which analyzes historical data to identify patterns and dependencies in a program's behavior. Specifically, Timeloops employs a combination of statistical methods and machine learning algorithms to discover these patterns, and then constructs a set of rules that accurately predict the program's subsequent actions. Our results demonstrate that Timeloops outperforms existing baselines in terms of precision and efficiency in predicting program behavior, and also in identifying the same set of system calls with lower computational resources.

This research extends the integrated probability density filter model by incorporating a discrete lattice-based target existence framework and continuous target state densities in relation to birth model management. The proposed algorithmic solutions are convolved at each time step, with the degree of computation依赖性 on the lattice size and filtering difficulty. The surface remains stable among lattice dimensions under localized birth scenarios and scales linearly with the lattice size in non-localized cases. The proposed method is demonstrated through simulation using real sensor data.
